The 30-year is thirty-two basis points above the 10-year and fifty-nine above the 2-year, a meaningful premium for duration and inflation uncertainty.

Latest official SOFR is 3.90 percent, effective Thursday. The New York Fed did not publish a newer effective rate before the weekend, so 3.90 is the correct current print. A floating-rate loan at SOFR plus 300 begins near 6.90 percent before floors, fees and cap cost. At SOFR plus 400, the simple starting coupon is 7.90 percent.

The split remains uncomfortable for borrowers. SOFR has hovered in the high threes while Treasury yields have climbed sharply. Floating-rate borrowers are receiving little benchmark relief, and fixed-rate borrowers are seeing proceeds and debt-service coverage squeezed by higher base rates. A lender can hold its spread steady and still deliver a materially worse coupon than it showed early in the week.

Deals are getting done, including in parts of multifamily where structure matters more than a perfect rate.

Rockland Trust provided a 10.67 million dollar construction loan for an income-restricted apartment development in Malden, Massachusetts. The Asian Community Development Corporation project will create twenty apartments on a former Salvation Army property. It is a modest loan beside the large transactions that usually make headlines, but it demonstrates a lane where relationship banks remain useful: local knowledge, public support and a clearly defined community housing plan.

In Miami, HALL Structured Finance closed a 29.4 million dollar first-mortgage construction loan for a new Class A apartment development. That is a different execution. A private lender is funding development risk in a major Sun Belt market, where the sponsor must carry construction, lease-up and supply risk at today’s cost of capital.

Those loans sit beside the deals already moving through the market. Bank OZK supplied 86 million dollars for a Broward County rental development, while Argentic funded a 39.1 million dollar floating-rate takeout for the completed, 173-unit Tennessen Flats in Wisconsin. Benefit Street’s 250 million dollar refinancing of Society Las Olas in Fort Lauderdale is the larger version of that completion-to-stabilization trade.

Together, the transactions show how the lender map is dividing. Banks are active where relationships, deposits, recourse or specialized construction experience improve the risk. Life companies are still best positioned for conservative leverage, durable income and fixed-rate certainty on stabilized assets. CMBS offers nonrecourse proceeds and scale when collateral can support securitization. Debt funds are earning their spread by accepting construction, lease-up, conversion and timing risk that permanent lenders generally will not take.

Execution tone is active but selective. Strong sponsors can obtain competing terms. The negotiation is moving beyond the headline spread to proceeds, interest-only periods, reserves, extension tests and the exact definition of stabilization. Borrowers with a near-term maturity should compare the cost of flexible bridge capital with the economic damage of forcing a permanent loan before income has matured.

Life-company execution is especially sensitive to duration today. A borrower choosing a five-, seven- or ten-year fixed-rate loan is choosing a different point on a steep curve, not simply a different maturity date. Life companies can still reward low leverage and strong coverage with disciplined pricing, but they are unlikely to stretch proceeds to win a marginal deal. Banks may offer more flexibility to an existing customer, though recourse, deposits and amortization can change the comparison. The useful exercise is to put every proposal on the same basis: net proceeds, annual debt service, required reserves, prepayment cost and cash needed at closing. A lower coupon is not automatically the lowest-cost execution.

CMBS brings that tradeoff into sharper focus. About 4.42 billion dollars of private-label CMBS debt reaches hard maturity in November, covering 182 whole loans. More than half of the balance has a debt yield below eight percent. Roughly eighty percent is fixed-rate debt carrying an average coupon of only 4.14 percent.

That gap explains why a current loan can still fail its refinancing test. Replacing a four-percent coupon with debt in the mid-sixes or higher can reduce proceeds even when property income has not fallen. A recent sizing analysis put the November refinancing gap near 805 million dollars. Extensions, fresh equity, note sales and paydowns will all be part of the solution.

The market can still finance strong collateral. Simon Property Group’s planned 555 million dollar Dadeland Mall refinancing is the type of large, performing retail loan that can attract CMBS demand. The harder cases are loans where occupancy has weakened, valuation has fallen or the maturity arrived before the business plan was complete. October’s national CMBS distress rate was 11.2 percent, with office representing the largest share of distressed balances.

For multifamily, agency liquidity remains the baseline even though higher Treasury yields have changed proceeds. Freddie Mac has just settled its 977 million dollar K-184 and 343 million dollar small-balance ML-38 securitizations. Those settlements recycle capacity and demonstrate continuing investor demand, but they do not insulate new borrowers from Friday’s benchmark levels.

Fannie Mae’s updated loan documents may now be used and become mandatory for most commitments dated December eighth or later. The revisions clarify treatment of preferred equity, structured common equity and certain investor guarantees. That matters when borrowers are using layered capital to close a proceeds gap. Fannie’s DUS Gateway workflow for credit-facility collateral releases is also live, moving that process into a more standardized system.

There was no meaningful new Freddie, Fannie or HUD multifamily policy announced over the weekend. HUD and FHA remain relevant because long-term, fully amortizing fixed-rate debt can remove refinancing risk. The tradeoff is process, including third-party reports, documentation and closing time. Current published apartment-loan screens show FHA roughly from 6.11 to 7.46 percent, Fannie from 5.46 to 6.26, Freddie from 5.76 to 9.23, CMBS from 6.98 to 8.65 and bridge debt from about 6 to 13 percent. Those are broad indications, not executable quotes.

Here is the concise markets snapshot. Friday’s Treasury close was 4.88 percent on the 2-year, 4.98 on the 5-year, 5.15 on the 10-year and 5.47 on the 30-year. Latest official SOFR is 3.90 percent effective November twelfth. The 5-year sits just below five percent, and the long end remains upward sloping.

One thing to watch Monday is not merely whether the 5-year crosses five percent, but how quickly lenders translate the opening move into quote sheets and proceeds. Retail sales and Federal Reserve minutes are ahead this week, so volatility may continue. Ask every lender to separate the benchmark, spread, floor, fees, cap assumptions and lock mechanics. In this market, the structure of the quote can matter as much as the quoted rate.

That is the Debt Desk for Sunday. Have a good morning.

item.title: Debt Desk — Debt Desk — November 14, 2026: Flight Chaos, a Five-Percent Curve and Active Private Credit
item.description: The Morning Brief covers the nationwide aviation shutdown, a Supreme Court asylum case, Alaska's historic governor result and a shift in Iran policy. Debt Desk tracks Friday's Treasury curve and SOFR, fresh bank and private-credit deals, CMBS execution, agency multifamily activity and HUD pricing.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It is Saturday, November fourteenth.

We begin with the national brief.

Airlines are trying to rebuild their schedules after the longest nationwide ground stop in twenty-five years. More than two thousand flights were canceled Saturday, after a communications failure stopped departures across the country for more than four hours Friday. The Federal Aviation Administration began allowing limited departures again around eight-fifteen Friday night, but the disruption carried straight into the weekend.

Administration officials say new technology being added to the air traffic control system overloaded older equipment and created intermittent communications and radar gaps. More than three thousand aircraft already in the air landed safely, and officials said passengers were not in danger. The scale of the outage still matters. This was only the second nationwide ground stop since the September eleventh attacks, and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy warned that more disruptions are possible while the system is modernized.

The failure also puts infrastructure spending back in focus. Congress approved twelve-and-a-half billion dollars for the current overhaul, which includes replacing copper lines with fiber and upgrading radio systems. The White House is seeking another thirty billion. For travelers, the near-term issue is whether airlines can get aircraft and crews back into position before the next wave of departures. Officials say the system should normalize before Thanksgiving, but Saturday's cancellation count shows that the recovery is not immediate.

The second story is a major immigration case headed to the Supreme Court. The justices agreed Friday to consider President Trump's executive order suspending access to asylum at the southern border. Lower courts found the order illegal, and the administration wants that judgment reversed.

Federal law says people may apply for asylum if they fear persecution, regardless of how they entered the country. The administration argues that the executive branch can categorically deny asylum to migrants covered by the order and should not be required to process applications it expects to reject. Immigration advocates say the order attempts to erase protections that Congress wrote into law.

The case will test how much discretion a president has when a statute creates an application process but leaves the executive branch authority over the final decision. It is also one of the clearest legal tests of the administration's broader immigration campaign. Watch the briefing schedule and whether the court keeps the policy in place while the appeal proceeds.

The third story is an electoral change in Alaska that would have been difficult to imagine a few years ago. Former state lawmaker Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins has become the first Democrat elected governor there since 1998. At thirty-seven, he will also be the youngest governor in Alaska history.

Kreiss-Tomkins defeated three Republicans under the state's ranked-choice voting system, including a candidate backed by President Trump. His campaign emphasized bipartisanship and local concerns rather than a purely national message. The result is part of the larger Democratic wave in the midterm elections, but Alaska gives it a distinctive shape: a normally Republican state used its unusual election system to choose a Democrat who presented himself as pragmatic.

The governing test comes next. Alaska's finances remain closely connected to energy revenue, while cost of living, public services and the annual Permanent Fund dividend create their own political pressures. The result also keeps ranked-choice voting in the national debate, since supporters see it as a way to reward broader coalitions and critics argue that it complicates elections.

The fourth story is a change in tone on Iran. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Friday that further American military action is not needed because economic pressure has weakened Iran. That follows a week of conflicting signals and unverified Iranian claims involving a U.S. radar site in Bahrain and a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz.

The new language does not settle the conflict, but it suggests that the administration is leaning toward economic isolation rather than another immediate round of strikes. That matters to energy and shipping markets because the Strait of Hormuz remains one of the world's most important oil routes. It also matters diplomatically ahead of next week's Asia-Pacific summit, where President Trump is expected to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The responsible reading is that Washington is signaling restraint without offering Iran relief. Watch whether Tehran answers with restraint of its own, whether maritime authorities confirm any new incident in the strait, and whether the three leaders use the summit to discuss a path away from escalation.

That is the national brief. Now to the Debt Desk.

The Treasury selloff continued into Friday's close. The official curve finished at 4.88 percent on the 2-year, 4.98 on the 5-year, 5.15 on the 10-year and 5.47 on the 30-year.

Compared with Thursday, the 2-year rose two basis points, the 5-year rose three, the 10-year rose five and the 30-year rose four. The larger weekly move is the real story. Since Monday, the 2-year has risen thirty-two basis points, the 5-year thirty-one, the 10-year twenty-seven and the 30-year twenty-one.

The curve is still upward sloping, but the term structure is doing different work at each point. The 2-year reflects a market that expects monetary policy to remain restrictive. The 5-year, now just two basis points below five percent, is pressing directly on the benchmark used for many commercial and multifamily fixed-rate quotes. The 10-year above 5.1 percent raises coupons for longer-term bank, agency and CMBS executions. The 30-year at 5.47 percent says long-duration capital still demands a substantial premium.

Latest official SOFR is 3.90 percent, effective Thursday, up one basis point from the prior published reading. A floating-rate loan at SOFR plus 300 starts near 6.90 percent before fees, floors and the cost of an interest-rate cap. At SOFR plus 400, the simple benchmark-and-spread calculation is 7.90 percent.

That leaves borrowers with an unusual split. SOFR has been broadly stable around the high threes, while intermediate and long Treasury yields have moved sharply higher. Floating-rate borrowers are not receiving meaningful benchmark relief, and fixed-rate borrowers are absorbing a rapid increase in base rates. Even when a lender holds its spread, the coupon can move enough in a few days to change debt-service coverage and proceeds.

Deals are still getting done. In South Florida, Bank OZK supplied an 86 million dollar construction loan for a Broward County rental project. That is a familiar role for the bank: large construction exposure on a project and sponsorship it understands, with tighter structure than borrowers might have found during the easiest part of the cycle. It is also evidence that banks have not abandoned development lending. They are choosing it more carefully.

In Manhattan, OakNorth and BridgeCity Capital provided an 83-and-a-half million dollar co-loan for CSC Real Estate's conversion of 136 East 57th Street from office space into 136 apartments. The twenty-story building dates to 1931 and sits near Lexington Avenue. This is private credit taking execution risk that is difficult for a conventional permanent lender to underwrite before construction and lease-up are complete.

The transaction also captures an important theme in office conversions. The opportunity is real, but the capital stack must absorb zoning, construction, design and timing risk before the building produces stabilized residential income. Debt funds and specialty banks can price that complexity. Life companies usually want to enter after completion, and CMBS is generally a takeout rather than a construction solution.

Another private-credit lender, Argentic, funded a 39.1 million dollar floating-rate construction takeout for Tennessen Flats, a 173-unit apartment community in Menomonee Falls, Wisconsin. JLL arranged the loan for Weas Development and Klein Development. The financing replaces the existing construction debt.

That is a smaller version of the Society Las Olas transaction we discussed yesterday. Benefit Street Partners refinanced that newly completed Fort Lauderdale tower with 250 million dollars, replacing 226 million of construction financing. In both cases, private lenders are bridging the period between physical completion and the operating history required for the best permanent execution.

The deals show why debt funds remain active even when their coupons look expensive. They can underwrite lease-up, conversion and business-plan risk while offering enough proceeds to retire construction debt. Borrowers pay for flexibility, but flexibility can be more valuable than the lowest headline rate when a maturity is approaching.

Banks, life companies, CMBS lenders and debt funds are therefore competing in different lanes. Banks are strongest with relationships, recourse and stabilized cash flow, while a few large construction lenders still pursue complex projects. Life companies remain disciplined on leverage and favor durable income, strong locations and fixed-rate certainty. CMBS can provide nonrecourse proceeds at scale, especially for stable assets that fit securitization. Debt funds are taking the transition risk, with spreads and fees that reflect it.

Published market indications Friday put good-quality apartment loans in a very wide range. Fannie Mae executions were roughly 5.46 to 6.26 percent, CMBS was roughly 6.98 to 8.65, bridge debt ranged from about 6 to 13 percent, and FHA loans were shown around 6.16 to 7.51 percent. Those are screening ranges, not executable quotes. Leverage, debt-service coverage, sponsor strength, market, amortization and prepayment terms can move a real proposal substantially.

In CMBS, the sharp Treasury move makes timing more important. A conduit lender may quote a stable spread and still deliver a higher all-in coupon as the 10-year rises. Strong collateral can still clear. Simon Property Group's planned 555 million dollar refinancing of Dadeland Mall is the kind of large, performing retail loan the market can absorb. But recent office liquidations in Washington and San Francisco show the other side of securitization: old losses are moving from appraisals into realized recoveries.

For borrowers, the key is to separate spread risk from benchmark risk. A spread lock does not necessarily lock the Treasury. A rate cap protects a floating loan only above its strike. A forward commitment can reduce timing risk, but it brings conditions. The details of the lock are now as important as the opening coupon.

Multifamily liquidity remains broad but segmented. The fresh Argentic takeout and Benefit Street refinance show debt funds moving completed projects toward stabilization. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac remain the baseline comparison for stabilized nonrecourse apartments. Freddie's 977 million dollar K-184 and 343 million dollar small-balance ML-38 securitizations reached their scheduled settlement this week, recycling lender capacity even as benchmarks moved higher.

Fannie Mae's new DUS Gateway workflow for credit-facility collateral releases also became available Thursday. That is an operational change, not a pricing program, but it should make portfolio administration more consistent for participating borrowers and lenders. There was no material new agency multifamily policy announced overnight.

There was also no material new HUD or FHA multifamily policy or major closing disclosed in the last day. HUD remains relevant because its long-term, fully amortizing fixed-rate structures can solve for duration and eliminate refinance risk. The tradeoff remains process: documentation, third-party reports and closing time can be heavier than with bank, agency or private-credit alternatives. Friday's broad FHA indication of 6.16 to 7.51 percent is only a starting point. Mortgage insurance, leverage, affordability requirements and the specific program determine the real economics.

Here is the concise markets snapshot. The Treasury curve closed Friday at 4.88 percent on the 2-year, 4.98 on the 5-year, 5.15 on the 10-year and 5.47 on the 30-year. Latest official SOFR is 3.90 percent for November twelfth. The 5-year is two basis points below five percent, the 10-year is seventeen basis points above the 5-year, and the 30-year is fifty-nine basis points above the 2-year.

One thing to watch when markets reopen Monday is whether the 5-year Treasury holds below five percent. A clean break above that level would not have magical economic meaning, but it would matter for borrower psychology, lender quote sheets and loan proceeds. Ask lenders to identify the benchmark timestamp, credit spread, floor, fees and lock mechanics separately. In a volatile market, a clear quote is worth almost as much as a low one.

That is the Debt Desk for Saturday. Have a good morning.

item.title: Debt Desk — Debt Desk — November 13, 2026: AI Fallout, a Steeper Curve and Fresh Private Credit
item.description: The Morning Brief covers Nvidia leadership fallout, a major crypto recovery, new congressional investigations and renewed tension around the Strait of Hormuz. Debt Desk tracks the Treasury curve, SOFR, fresh C-PACE and multifamily refinancings, CMBS stress, agency execution and HUD pricing.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It is Friday, November thirteenth.

We begin with the national brief.

The abrupt resignation of Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang is sending a new wave of uncertainty through the artificial intelligence economy. Huang stepped down Thursday after the disclosure of an affair with a businesswoman accused of acting as an agent for China. Lawmakers still want him to appear for a briefing about those contacts, and the immediate market reaction spread well beyond Nvidia.

CoreWeave, which buys Nvidia chips and rents computing capacity to AI customers, fell nearly seven percent Thursday. Nvidia owns almost thirteen percent of that company. Analysts are now looking again at the circular relationships that connect chipmakers, data-center operators, cloud companies and heavily financed AI startups.

That matters because the AI boom has been built on more than software demand. It has pulled enormous amounts of capital into chips, power infrastructure, data centers and private-company valuations. A leadership crisis at the industry's most important supplier does not erase those needs, but it can make investors less willing to accept optimistic forecasts or financing structures that depend on one another. The next test is whether the selloff stays concentrated in a few connected companies or becomes a broader reassessment of AI spending and credit.

The second story is a major recovery from the largest cryptocurrency theft on record. The FBI says the United States has seized more than one-point-two billion dollars of crypto stolen from Binance last month. The full theft totaled about six-point-three billion dollars, and U.S. officials have attributed it to a North Korean hacking group known as TraderTraitor.

Government agencies and private companies have frozen more than two-point-seven billion dollars of the stolen assets so far. The Justice Department now has court authorization to seize or restrain part of that amount. A judge will ultimately sort through competing claims before recovered funds can be returned.

The FBI also blamed North Korea for a separate social-engineering campaign that stole about four hundred million dollars over eighteen months. That operation allegedly used hijacked messaging accounts and deepfake video. The broader point is that cryptocurrency theft is now both a financial-crime problem and a national-security problem. Officials say North Korea uses the proceeds to support its weapons programs, while the speed of blockchain transfers makes the first hours after a breach critical.

The third story is an early example of the congressional investigations expected after Democrats won control of both chambers. Senators Ron Wyden and Angela Alsobrooks have opened an inquiry into whether Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Junior misled Congress about a 2019 trip to Samoa. They asked Children's Health Defense, the anti-vaccine organization Kennedy once chaired, for documents involving the trip, his presidential campaign and his confirmation process.

The inquiry follows reporting by the Associated Press and The Guardian that challenged Kennedy's testimony that the Samoa trip had nothing to do with vaccines. It also makes yesterday's broader oversight confrontation more concrete. The White House has warned incoming House investigators against what it calls intimidation, while Democrats say they intend to use subpoena and hearing powers aggressively.

This investigation begins with document requests, not a finding of wrongdoing. But it shows that the incoming majority is not waiting until January to identify targets and build records. Watch for whether the organization complies, whether Kennedy is asked to testify again and whether the dispute expands into a larger review of health policy and confirmation testimony.

The fourth story is renewed tension around the Strait of Hormuz. Iran's Revolutionary Guard says it destroyed a U.S. early-warning radar in Bahrain after an American strike on a telecommunications pole in southern Iran. It separately says a liquefied-petroleum-gas tanker struck a mine in the strait after ignoring Iranian warnings.

Neither claim had been independently verified early Friday, and U.S. Central Command and Bahrain had not immediately confirmed the radar incident. That uncertainty is important. The claims are serious because Bahrain hosts the U.S. Navy's Fifth Fleet, and the Strait of Hormuz is a critical route for global energy shipments. They are not yet confirmed facts.

The practical risk is escalation through a cycle of strikes, disputed shipping incidents and retaliation. Energy and freight markets will focus on any confirmation from the United States, Bahrain or independent maritime monitors. Until then, the responsible reading is that Iran has raised the level of its public claims, while the evidence is still catching up.

That is the national brief. Now to the Debt Desk.

The Treasury curve moved sharply higher in the first full session after Veterans Day. At Thursday's official close, the 2-year yield was 4.86 percent, the 5-year was 4.95, the 10-year was 5.10 and the 30-year was 5.43.

Compared with Tuesday, that is another thirteen basis points on the 2-year, fourteen on the 5-year, twelve on the 10-year and eight on the 30-year. The curve remains upward sloping, with nine basis points between the 2-year and 5-year, fifteen between the 5-year and 10-year, and thirty-three between the 10-year and 30-year.

For borrowers, the move is broader than a headline about the 10-year. Five-year fixed-rate quotes now start from a benchmark near five percent, and the long bond above 5.4 percent keeps pressure on long-duration capital. The front end also rose, reflecting concern that inflation could keep Federal Reserve policy restrictive.

Latest official SOFR is 3.89 percent, effective Tuesday, up one basis point from Monday but down five basis points from November fourth. A floating-rate loan at SOFR plus 300 begins near 6.89 percent before fees, floors and cap costs. At SOFR plus 400, the benchmark-and-spread calculation is 7.89 percent.

So the split we described yesterday has become more pronounced. Floating-rate borrowers have received a small amount of recent benchmark relief. Fixed-rate borrowers have seen Treasury yields climb much faster. A lender may hold its credit spread unchanged and still deliver a meaningfully higher coupon than it quoted earlier in the week.

Deals are still getting done, and one fresh transaction shows how borrowers are widening the capital-source map. Jay Paul Company closed 227.5 million dollars of commercial property assessed clean energy financing from Nuveen Green Capital for Springdale Green, an 881,000-square-foot office campus in Austin.

The C-PACE loan refinances prior construction debt and recaptures eligible spending on energy and water improvements. It is the largest C-PACE financing completed in Texas. Springdale Green was substantially completed almost two years ago and is still working through lease-up in a difficult office market.

That is precisely why the structure matters. Long-term, fixed-rate C-PACE capital can give a sponsor more time to lease a transitional asset without forcing a conventional refinancing before the business plan is mature. It is not a universal solution, because the assessment remains attached to the property and must fit alongside other creditors. But at this scale, C-PACE is no longer a niche footnote. It is functioning as core recapitalization capital.

Private credit also delivered a clean multifamily handoff. PMG and Greybook secured a 250 million dollar refinance from Benefit Street Partners for the second phase of Society Las Olas in downtown Fort Lauderdale. The 42-story, 563-unit tower was completed this year. The new loan replaces 226 million dollars of construction financing from Related Fund Management and Lubert-Adler.

This is the kind of transaction debt funds are positioned to win: a newly completed building with lease-up history still developing, a large loan balance and a sponsor that needs a bridge from construction to stabilization. The higher proceeds also suggest the refinance is doing more than simply replacing the old principal. The lender is underwriting the value of a completed asset while accepting operating risk that many banks or life companies would prefer to revisit after occupancy matures.

Banks remain active, but the credit box is clearest on stabilized assets, strong sponsors and relationship opportunities. Live lender-network indications today put five-year bank multifamily coupons around 6.88 percent on average, with agency multifamily around 6.26 and five-year CMBS around 7.15. Those are broad comparison figures, not executable quotes, and individual deals can vary widely by leverage, debt-service coverage, market and structure.

The direction is more useful than the decimal. Banks can compete hard when deposits and relationships support the loan. Life companies remain focused on conservative leverage, durable cash flow and fixed-rate certainty. Debt funds accept more transition and complexity but charge for that flexibility. CMBS offers nonrecourse proceeds and scale, though today's benchmark move can raise the all-in coupon quickly.

Fresh survey data reinforces that picture. Commercial real estate financing activity rose thirteen percent from the second quarter to the third, with a notable increase in construction quotes for multifamily and industrial projects. At the same time, spreads widened on ground-up construction across nearly every loan category, and all-in costs rose across most property and product types. Capital is available. It is not cheap, and construction risk is being priced explicitly.

In CMBS, the market is still showing both capacity and loss recognition. The planned 555 million dollar Dadeland Mall refinance remains an example of securitization supporting a dominant, high-performing retail asset. On the stress side, the securitized loan on 1615 L Street in Washington was resolved through a receivership sale for 45 million dollars against debt of roughly 134 million. A San Francisco office loan tied to 225 Bush was liquidated with a loss of almost 140 million dollars.

Those outcomes are reminders that special servicing is not only about extensions. Older office loans can move from appraisal reductions to realized losses when occupancy and sale value fail to recover. At the same time, strong assets are still accessing new CMBS capital. The market is clearing through dispersion rather than through one uniform recovery.

Multifamily has the same split. The Society Las Olas refinance shows large private-credit demand for a newly delivered rental tower. Freddie Mac's 977 million dollar K-184 and 343 million dollar small-balance ML-38 transactions reached their scheduled closing yesterday, moving completed loans through the agency securitization channel. Fannie Mae also put its DUS Gateway collateral-release workflow into effect, making portfolio administration more standardized for credit-facility borrowers.

There was no material new Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac or HUD policy announcement in the last day. For stabilized apartments, the agencies remain the baseline nonrecourse comparison. For lease-up and heavier execution risk, debt funds can move earlier. For eligible construction, substantial rehabilitation and affordable housing, HUD and FHA still offer long-term, fully amortizing fixed-rate debt, but the borrower trades speed for documentation and process.

Indicative FHA multifamily pricing published Thursday ranged from about 6.08 to 7.43 percent before deal-specific adjustments, while current 223(f) indications from a major mortgage-banking rate sheet were in the high-sixes including mortgage insurance. Those numbers are useful for screening, not a commitment. Borrowers should compare the mortgage-insurance premium, amortization, prepayment structure and expected closing timeline alongside the coupon.

Here is the concise markets snapshot. The official Treasury curve closed Thursday at 4.86 percent on the 2-year, 4.95 on the 5-year, 5.10 on the 10-year and 5.43 on the 30-year. Latest official SOFR is 3.89 percent for November tenth. The 5-year rose fourteen basis points in the latest session, and the 30-year sits fifty-seven basis points above the 2-year. Broad equity indexes finished lower Thursday as investors reassessed AI exposure.

One thing to watch today is the 5-year Treasury. It is now only five basis points below five percent, and that area matters directly for many commercial and multifamily loan quotes. If the 5-year breaks decisively above five percent, lenders may shorten rate-lock windows, trim proceeds or require borrowers to accept a higher coupon. If it settles back, the market gets a chance to rebuild quotes after a volatile week. Ask for the benchmark timestamp, the spread and the lock mechanics separately.

That is the Debt Desk for Friday. Have a good morning.

item.title: Debt Desk — Debt Desk — November 12, 2026: Election Aftershocks and Fresh Capital Across the Stack
item.description: A historic Mississippi Senate result, new SNAP restrictions, Ukraine diplomacy and a White House oversight fight lead the Morning Brief. Debt Desk covers the post-CPI curve, SOFR, fresh bank and private-credit deals, CMBS, agency multifamily activity and HUD execution.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It is Thursday, November twelfth.

We begin with the national brief.

Democrat Scott Colom has won the U.S. Senate race in Mississippi, becoming the state’s first Black senator since Reconstruction and giving Democrats fifty-five seats in the next Congress. The Associated Press called the race Wednesday evening after a new batch of votes from Jackson County left Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith without a realistic path back. She later conceded.

Colom’s margin was narrow, about forty-seven hundred votes out of more than nine hundred sixty-two thousand counted when the race was called. But the political meaning is much larger. Democrats will enter January with a net gain of eight Senate seats, their strongest midterm gain in the chamber since 1986. They will also control the House.

That gives the incoming majority room to move legislation, shape nominations and run investigations without depending on the most vulnerable member for every vote. It also confirms that last week’s backlash reached well beyond the usual swing states. Mississippi has not sent a Democrat to the Senate in decades. Counties must certify results by Friday, but the remaining ballots are not expected to change the winner.

The second story is a new Trump administration proposal that would make it harder for some households to receive federal grocery assistance. The Agriculture Department wants to end a practice that lets states use eligibility for certain Temporary Assistance for Needy Families benefits to qualify households automatically for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP.

The administration says it is closing a loophole. Critics say the rule would remove flexibility that states use to reach working families whose income or assets might otherwise put them outside the standard SNAP test. The program served thirty-six million people as of July, roughly one in ten Americans, and participation was already down thirteen percent from a year earlier.

The proposal also connects to school meals. The Agriculture Department estimates that nearly one-point-eight million children would lose automatic meal eligibility when their families lose SNAP. Most would still qualify for free or reduced-price meals under a separate application, but some families may not complete that extra step. States are also preparing to shoulder a larger share of SNAP administrative costs under last year’s tax and policy law. So this is not only a benefit question for households. It is a budget and implementation question for governors and state agencies.

The third story is a concrete, if limited, result from the Russia-Ukraine talks we have been following. Two days of U.S.-mediated negotiations in Abu Dhabi ended Wednesday with an agreement on a large prisoner exchange. There was no visible breakthrough on territory or on a broader end to the war, but the exchange gives the process an outcome that can be measured.

American envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner traveled to Moscow Thursday to brief President Vladimir Putin and discuss the next steps. They are then expected to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Dublin. Zelenskyy welcomed the prisoner agreement but again rejected any settlement that requires Ukraine to surrender occupied territory.

The diplomatic sequence matters. The talks have moved from one room in Abu Dhabi to direct follow-ups with both presidents, which keeps the channel alive. But the central dispute is unchanged, and fighting continues. The next test is whether the prisoner exchange is completed and whether Moscow and Kyiv authorize another negotiating round with a defined agenda. Humanitarian progress is real progress. It is not the same thing as a peace framework.

The fourth story is an early confrontation over the powers of the next Congress. White House counsel Will Scharf warned Representative Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, that investigations designed to intimidate executive branch officials could cross into what he called blatant criminality. Garcia said the warning would not deter congressional oversight.

The letter is notable because Democrats do not take control until January, yet the institutional fight has already started. The House can issue subpoenas, hold hearings and compel testimony as part of its oversight role. The White House can assert privileges, resist requests and challenge subpoenas in court. The language from both sides suggests those disputes could begin quickly.

For listeners, the practical point is that the midterm result is already changing behavior in Washington. The Hegseth impeachment effort was blocked this week, closing that immediate personnel fight. Attention is now shifting toward the broader investigations the incoming majority may pursue into the Iran war, contracting, ethics and administration decision-making.

That is the national brief. Now to the Debt Desk.

The bond market reopens today after Veterans Day with Tuesday’s inflation selloff as the starting point. At the latest official Treasury close, the 2-year yield was 4.73 percent, the 5-year was 4.81, the 10-year was 4.98 and the 30-year was 5.35.

That is an upward-sloping curve, but the inflation shock hit the front end hardest. On Tuesday, the 2-year rose seventeen basis points, the 5-year rose fourteen, the 10-year rose ten and the 30-year rose nine. The shape tells us the market increased the odds of tighter Federal Reserve policy while still demanding a substantial long-term premium for inflation and government borrowing.

For commercial real estate, the 5-year remains especially important. It is a common index for bank, life-company, agency and securitized executions. The 30-year matters too, even when a loan does not price directly from it, because a 5.35 percent long bond makes it harder to argue that long-duration capital should become cheap quickly.

Latest official SOFR is 3.88 percent, effective Monday, unchanged from the last figure available during the holiday. That puts a floating-rate loan at SOFR plus 300 basis points near 6.88 percent before floors, fees and the cost of an interest-rate cap. At SOFR plus 400, the starting benchmark-and-spread cost is about 7.88 percent.

The distinction this morning is simple. SOFR has eased from its early-November level, helping existing floating-rate borrowers a little, while Treasury yields jumped after inflation, making fresh fixed-rate execution more expensive. Today’s live market will show whether investors treat Tuesday as a complete repricing or the first leg of a larger move.

Deals are getting done across several parts of the capital stack. A joint venture led by CP Group secured 271.5 million dollars from Blackstone Real Estate Debt Strategies for its acquisition and renovation of Mizner Park in Boca Raton. The mixed-use property includes 272 apartments, roughly 268,000 square feet of office and about 276,000 square feet of retail.

The sponsors paid 193 million dollars for the property interests, and the financing exceeds that purchase amount because the business plan includes upgrades to facades, landscaping, infrastructure and common areas. This is private credit funding acquisition plus future value creation across three property types. It also shows why debt funds remain relevant even when banks are lending: a transitional mixed-use plan often needs more flexibility than a conventional balance-sheet mortgage offers.

Private credit also showed up in office. RFR refinanced 100 Biscayne in downtown Miami with a 101 million dollar loan from Derby Lane Partners and Axonic Capital. RFR bought the building in 2022 for 90 million dollars and says it increased occupancy from below sixty percent to roughly ninety percent by leasing about 248,000 square feet.

That is the kind of office story lenders can finance today. The building is not being underwritten on hope alone. The sponsor completed a repositioning, improved occupancy and assembled a tenant roster that includes large corporate users. The capital still came from alternative lenders, which tells us even a stronger office refinance may sit outside many banks’ preferred credit box.

Banks are not absent. Citibank provided a 104 million dollar refinance for AYA New York’s 233-unit Manhattan apartment portfolio, covering Renoir House on the Upper East Side and 120 to 125 Riverside Drive on the Upper West Side. The owner has upgraded apartments and common areas and restored the Riverside building’s historic facade.

That transaction fits the bank lane: established urban multifamily, existing cash flow, completed improvements and a borrower with a concentrated local portfolio. Banks remain selective, but they can be aggressive on stabilized assets where they understand the market and want the relationship.

Life companies continue to compete in that same low-leverage, stabilized space, particularly for borrowers who value fixed-rate certainty and long duration. There was not a newly disclosed life-company closing in the last day strong enough to lead today’s coverage. The execution tone, however, is consistent: life companies can offer attractive spreads on high-quality collateral, but the Treasury move can still raise the all-in coupon even when the credit spread is unchanged.

CMBS offers the clearest large-loan scale. A developing transaction we are watching is the planned 555 million dollar refinance of Dadeland Mall in South Florida. Wells Fargo, Bank of Montreal and JPMorgan are originating the ten-year, fixed-rate, interest-only loan for Simon Property Group and Prime Property Fund. The package is expected to refinance 345 million dollars of existing debt and return nearly 200 million dollars of equity to the sponsors.

Fitch valued the nearly full mall at 909 million dollars and reported rising net operating income through the latest twelve-month period. This is a strong-mall execution, not a blanket endorsement of retail. It sits in sharp contrast to Bridgewater Commons in New Jersey, where a 235 million dollar CMBS loan went to special servicing after failing its debt-yield requirement despite asset sales and a principal paydown.

That contrast is the CMBS market in miniature. Capital is available for dominant assets with durable cash flow, and securitization can support proceeds that relationship lenders may not. But maturity stress remains visible in older deals where performance does not meet extension tests. Investors are separating properties, sponsors and structures rather than making a single call on an entire sector.

In multifamily, the fresh bank refinance in Manhattan joins a still-active agency market. Freddie Mac’s 977 million dollar K-184 transaction and its 343 million dollar small-balance ML-38 transaction are scheduled to close today. Both priced last week, so today’s significance is settlement and capital-market completion rather than a new spread discovery.

Fannie Mae also puts a servicing change into effect today. DUS lenders can now process credit-facility collateral release requests through DUS Gateway, including selecting properties, specifying paydown order and reviewing the release price. That is operational plumbing, not a new loan product, but it can make portfolio management more standardized for borrowers using multi-asset credit facilities.

Together, those developments show the agency channel working at both ends. Freddie is moving loans through securitization, while Fannie is improving how existing credit facilities are managed. For new borrowers, Fannie and Freddie remain strong options for stabilized multifamily, especially when proceeds, amortization and nonrecourse structure matter more than the fastest possible closing.

Debt funds remain the more flexible choice for lease-up, renovation, construction and complicated capital stacks. The Blackstone financing at Mizner Park is the freshest example. The tradeoff is price. Private lenders may solve for future funding and complexity, but their spreads, fees and exit requirements generally demand a credible path to stabilization or sale.

HUD and FHA remain the long-duration lane for construction, substantial rehabilitation and eligible affordable or workforce housing. There was no material new FHA multifamily policy or disclosed closing in the last twenty-four hours. The active comparison is still execution certainty versus process: HUD can deliver fully amortizing, fixed-rate insured debt, but borrowers must plan for documentation, third-party reports and a longer approval path. That makes it a strategic choice, not a last-minute replacement for a bank or debt-fund bridge.

Here is the concise markets snapshot. The latest official Treasury curve is 4.73 percent on the 2-year, 4.81 percent on the 5-year, 4.98 percent on the 10-year and 5.35 percent on the 30-year. The latest official SOFR print is 3.88 percent for November 9. The 5-year sits eight basis points above the 2-year, while the 30-year is sixty-two basis points above it. Fixed-rate borrowers face a higher base after CPI, while floating-rate borrowers have received only modest recent relief.

One thing to watch today is how the reopened Treasury market handles that inflation repricing. If the 5-year and 10-year hold near Tuesday’s close, lenders can begin rebuilding quotes around a new base. If yields push higher again, borrowers should expect tighter rate-lock windows, more conservative proceeds and renewed pressure to buy down leverage. Ask for the spread and the index separately, and confirm exactly when each can lock.

That is the Debt Desk for Thursday. Have a good morning.

item.title: Debt Desk — Debt Desk — November 11, 2026: Inflation Reprices the Curve and Multifamily Deals Clear
item.description: Hot October inflation, a resolved Hegseth vote and a second day of Ukraine talks lead the Morning Brief. Debt Desk covers the Treasury selloff, lower SOFR, bank and private-credit executions, CMBS pricing, Fannie Mae activity and HUD financing.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It is Wednesday, November eleventh, and Veterans Day.

We begin with the national brief.

Inflation came in hotter than markets wanted, and the details show price pressure spreading beyond gasoline. The consumer price index rose four-tenths of one percent in October after a six-tenths increase in September. Core prices, excluding food and energy, rose three-tenths for a third straight month.

There is no official twelve-month October inflation rate because the government shutdown last year prevented the collection of October 2025 data. That makes the monthly composition especially important. Shelter rose three-tenths and accounted for more than thirty percent of the overall increase. Food rose five-tenths. Energy rose seven-tenths after a much larger jump in September. Medical care, recreation, insurance and household furnishings also moved higher.

For households, that means the inflation story is no longer only about oil and the Iran conflict. Food at home rose four-tenths, food away from home rose five-tenths, and several service categories accelerated. For the Federal Reserve, it is another month with core inflation running too fast for comfort.

Fed Governor Christopher Waller had already warned that a stronger policy move could be needed if core inflation remained at three-tenths or higher. Tuesday’s report met that test. It does not guarantee a larger rate increase, but it moved the burden of proof. Markets now need several softer reports, not one, before the Fed can credibly step back.

The second story is that House Republicans blocked the effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. This is a meaningful update from yesterday, when the vote count was still uncertain. Most Republicans stayed with the administration after President Trump publicly backed Hegseth, and the House halted Representative Thomas Massie’s resolution.

The vote closes the immediate threat to Hegseth, but not the argument behind it. His handling of the Iran war remains unpopular, the conflict contributed to higher fuel prices, and Republicans are still processing the midterm losses that cost them control of Congress. Hegseth used his first Pentagon news conference in six months to defend the administration’s military decisions. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Hegseth was carrying out the president’s orders.

The political consequence now moves from removal to oversight. Democrats take control of Congress in January. They will have subpoena power, committee gavels and an incentive to examine the war, military readiness and the administration’s decision-making. Tuesday’s vote resolved the personnel question for now. It did not settle the policy fight.

The third story is a second day of U.S.-brokered talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi. The delegations met for roughly four hours Tuesday and returned Wednesday for three-way talks with the United States. Ukraine is also consulting European, European Union and NATO officials who are in the city.

The first session focused on humanitarian issues, including prisoner exchanges, civilians in captivity and Ukrainian children taken into Russia. Security guarantees were also discussed. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the meeting constructive and substantive, while Rubio called it productive but warned that a breakthrough will take time.

The central divide remains intact. Ukraine says Europe must be part of a durable settlement because European governments would help provide security guarantees. Russia does not want Europe in the direct negotiations. Neither side has shown a willingness to compromise on territory, and the fighting continues. Russian strikes wounded civilians in Zaporizhzhia and Kharkiv, while Ukrainian drones hit the Russian port of Ust-Luga, a major oil-export facility.

The test today is not a sweeping peace agreement. It is whether the parties can turn the talks into a continuing process with specific work on humanitarian exchanges and security. That would be limited progress, but it would be more durable than another meeting that ends without a next step.

The fourth story is the continuing security risk around Iran even as the White House emphasizes diplomacy. The U.S. Air Force moved aircraft away from a base in England after a reported threat, and American forces remain positioned across the region. That action is a reminder that President Trump’s softer language has not produced a formal settlement or a military drawdown.

Qatar is still carrying proposals between Washington and Tehran. Markets have welcomed the possibility that renewed attacks are less likely, but Iran has not accepted Washington’s nuclear conditions, and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains central to the global energy outlook. The practical distinction is between reduced odds of immediate escalation and an actual end to the conflict. We have the first, not yet the second.

That is the national brief. Now to the Debt Desk.

The inflation report delivered a sharp repricing across the Treasury curve. At Tuesday’s official close, the 2-year yield was 4.73 percent, the 5-year was 4.81, the 10-year was 4.98 and the 30-year was 5.35.

Compared with Monday, the 2-year jumped seventeen basis points, the 5-year rose fourteen, the 10-year rose ten and the 30-year rose nine. The move was largest at the front end because hot inflation changes the expected path of Federal Reserve policy first. But this was not only a front-end event. Every major term point moved higher, lifting the base cost for short, intermediate and long-duration real estate debt.

The curve is still upward sloping. The 5-year is eight basis points above the 2-year. The 10-year is twenty-five basis points above it, and the 30-year is sixty-two basis points above it. That is a smaller 2-to-10 and 2-to-30 slope than Monday because the 2-year sold off hardest.

For borrowers, the 5-year move deserves special attention. Five-year bank, life-company, agency and CMBS executions often price from that part of the curve. A fourteen-basis-point increase in the index can erase a meaningful portion of a negotiated spread improvement. On a fifty-million-dollar, five-year interest-only loan, fourteen basis points is about seventy thousand dollars of additional annual interest.

Latest published SOFR moved the other way. It is 3.88 percent effective November ninth, down one basis point from the prior print and nine basis points from November third. A floating-rate loan at SOFR plus 300 basis points starts around 6.88 percent before floors, fees and cap costs. At SOFR plus 400, it starts around 7.88 percent.

That small SOFR decline helps existing floaters at the margin, but the CPI report raises a larger question: how long will the benchmark remain near this level, and will the Fed move it higher? Borrowers should not confuse a one-basis-point daily improvement with a change in the policy outlook.

Deals are still getting done, and Tuesday produced a useful example from the bank and private-credit sides of the market. Capstone Equities bought a ninety-five-million-dollar nonperforming loan backed by Garden City Plaza, a six-hundred-thousand-square-foot office complex on Long Island. Capstone paid fifty-one million dollars for the note, which had been held by Bank of America. Maxim Capital provided forty-one million dollars of note-on-note financing for the purchase.

That structure says a great deal about current execution. A bank is reducing exposure to troubled office collateral at a discount. A private investor is buying control through the debt. And an alternative lender is financing the discounted note rather than underwriting a conventional mortgage at the old property value. This is capital moving, but it is resolution capital, not a return to business as usual for challenged office loans.

Banks remain most competitive on clean, relationship-driven loans where deposits and other business support the return. They are also willing to sell or restructure exposures that no longer fit. Life companies are competing hard for stabilized, low-leverage assets, especially when borrowers want fixed-rate certainty. Their credit box is wider than it was during the most defensive part of the cycle, but it is still selective on office and transitional properties.

CMBS remains the scalable outlet for larger or nonrelationship loans. The latest weekly pricing shows both depth and discrimination. Four private-label transactions totaling 4.95 billion dollars priced in the week ended November sixth. Blackstone’s 3.34 billion dollar refinancing of twenty-nine AIR Communities apartment properties was the largest private-label deal of 2026. Its senior floating-rate class priced at SOFR plus 160 basis points, right on initial guidance and five basis points inside the recent three-month average.

A separate 549-million-dollar Sun Belt apartment refinancing priced its senior class at SOFR plus 195. The difference between those two prints is the market assigning value to scale, collateral quality, sponsorship and structure. Investors are available, but they are not treating every multifamily pool the same.

The latest ten-year conduit priced its senior benchmark class at eighty-eight basis points over Treasuries. That was eight basis points wider than the prior ten-year conduit and seven wider than the recent average. In plain English, the securitization market can clear large volume, but conduit execution has not tightened in a straight line.

For fixed-rate borrowers, Tuesday’s Treasury selloff matters on top of those spreads. A conduit quote that looked competitive Monday can carry a noticeably higher all-in coupon after the index move. For floating-rate single-asset deals, the current 3.88 percent SOFR print plus a 160 spread implies a starting benchmark-and-spread cost near 5.48 percent before fees and hedging. At SOFR plus 195, it is about 5.83 percent.

Debt funds continue to fill the gaps between bank, agency and securitized credit. They can finance transition, future funding and complex collateral, and they can move quickly. The Garden City note financing is one version of that role. The continuing watch item is warehouse leverage. Many debt funds rely on bank credit lines, so bank discipline still sits underneath a portion of private credit even when the loan itself comes from a nonbank lender.

Multifamily had a fresh agency execution Tuesday. Greystone provided 39.2 million dollars of fixed-rate Fannie Mae financing for Greybrook Realty Partners’ acquisition of Evolv, a 334-unit property in Mansfield, Texas, in the Dallas-Fort Worth area. The loan has a five-year term, three years of interest-only payments and then a thirty-five-year amortization schedule.

That is a clear example of agency liquidity supporting a real transaction, not only a refinance. The interest-only period helps near-term cash flow, while the long amortization after year three reduces the scheduled payment relative to a shorter conventional schedule. The five-year term also places the deal directly in the part of the curve that repriced sharply Tuesday, which makes the timing and mechanics of the rate lock important.

The broader agency market issued 3.6 billion dollars last week. Fannie Mae accounted for 399 million across seventeen pools. Freddie Mac issued 2.8 billion, including a 977-million-dollar K-deal and a 343-million-dollar small-balance transaction, plus multifamily participation certificates. Ginnie Mae added 418 million through twenty multifamily pools.

Freddie’s ten-year K-deal had a weighted-average coupon of 5.55 percent, loan-to-value of 61.6 percent and debt-service coverage of 1.52 times. Its senior bonds priced only a few basis points wider than recent averages. That shows the agency machine functioning efficiently, but the underlying coupon is a reminder that efficient securitization cannot remove the higher base-rate environment.

HUD and FHA remain important for construction, substantial rehabilitation and borrowers seeking fully amortizing, long-duration debt. There was no newly announced HUD closing in the last twenty-four hours strong enough to replace the agency deal as today’s lead. The active program story remains HUD’s expedited path for qualifying low-income housing tax credit transactions under Section 221 d 4, including eligible four-percent tax-credit projects.

That program can offer high leverage and long-term fixed-rate execution, but timing and documentation remain the tradeoff. The next meaningful proof point is a disclosed firm commitment or closing that demonstrates the faster process in practice. Until then, borrowers should underwrite HUD as a distinct execution path, not as a quick substitute for a bank bridge or an agency acquisition loan.

Here is the concise markets snapshot. Tuesday’s official Treasury close was 4.73 percent on the 2-year, 4.81 on the 5-year, 4.98 on the 10-year and 5.35 on the 30-year. Latest SOFR is 3.88 percent. October CPI rose four-tenths overall and three-tenths at the core. The bond market is closed today for Veterans Day, so Tuesday’s official curve remains the cleanest benchmark for live debt conversations.

One thing to watch is Friday’s producer price report. After hot consumer inflation, lenders and borrowers will look for evidence that pipeline costs are also accelerating. Until then, assume fixed-rate quotes are carrying Tuesday’s higher Treasury base, confirm exactly when the index can lock, and do not treat a tight credit spread as protection from a moving curve.

That is the Debt Desk for Wednesday. To everyone who served, thank you. Have a good morning.

item.title: Debt Desk — Debt Desk — November 10, 2026: Diplomacy Moves, Inflation Looms and CRE Credit Splits
item.description: Iran war rhetoric softens, Ukraine talks begin and Washington faces an impeachment fight. Debt Desk covers the latest Treasury curve and SOFR, a divided lending market, new multifamily financing, a record 2026 CMBS deal, agency activity and HUD.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It is Tuesday, November tenth.

The national brief begins with a significant change in President Trump’s language on Iran. After meeting Qatar’s prime minister Monday, Trump said the war is, in his words, militarily effectively over. He said renewed military action does not appear necessary for now and described positive momentum toward a longer-term solution.

That does not mean the conflict is over. The United States is maintaining its naval blockade, thousands of American troops remain in the region, and Iran has not publicly accepted the conditions Washington is seeking for its nuclear program. Trump has stepped back from escalation at several earlier moments, only for tensions to rise again.

Still, this is the clearest signal since the midterm election that the administration wants diplomacy to take the lead. Qatar has been carrying proposals between Washington and Tehran. The immediate test is whether those indirect talks produce a defined negotiating framework, rather than another temporary pause.

The economic stakes are substantial. Eight months of war and disruption around the Strait of Hormuz have pushed up fuel and shipping costs. Oil prices fell and stocks rose Monday as investors gave more weight to the possibility of de-escalation. Any durable opening could ease an important source of inflation. A breakdown could reverse that relief quickly.

The second story is the opening of U.S.-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi. This is a meaningful step beyond yesterday’s announcement because the delegations are now at the table. Ukraine began the day meeting American envoys along with representatives from the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, NATO and the European Commission. The Russian delegation arrived with a larger team than in earlier rounds.

Security guarantees are the central issue. Ukraine wants commitments that would deter or answer another Russian attack. Russia wants restrictions on Ukraine’s military, territorial concessions and limits on Europe’s role. Those positions remain far apart. Russia is also intensifying attacks on Ukraine’s power grid as winter approaches, while Ukraine has increased drone strikes on Russian oil refineries.

The presence of European and NATO officials matters because any credible guarantee would probably require their money, weapons and political commitment. The first thing to watch is whether Russia accepts Europe as part of the process. The larger test is whether the parties can move from broad language about peace to enforceable terms.

The third story is an impeachment effort against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Republican Representative Thomas Massie filed the resolution, and House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries supports it. A House vote could come by midweek. Democrats do not take control until January, but Massie would need only a small number of Republican votes if most Democrats remain united.

Hegseth is scheduled to hold his first Pentagon news conference in more than six months today. He says he welcomes a fight over the administration’s military decisions in Iran, Yemen and Venezuela. Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are defending him.

The timing connects the impeachment push to the election result. Voters rejected the Iran war by a wide margin, and Democrats won both chambers of Congress. Even if the current Republican Senate would not convict Hegseth, a House vote would force lawmakers to take a position and could preview the oversight battles coming next year.

The fourth story is the administration’s mixed post-election message on immigration. After suggesting Sunday that his deportation policy may have been too tough, Trump said Monday that the policy has not changed, called it very strong and ruled out amnesty. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Democrats have contacted him about working together, but no concrete proposal exists.

At the same time, the Supreme Court cleared the administration to resume border barrier work in the Big Bend region of Texas while a legal challenge continues. The decision pauses a lower-court order that had stopped construction. Opponents include environmental groups, local landowners and politicians from both parties. They argue that the region has low migrant traffic and that surveillance would be less damaging than new roads and barriers.

Taken together, the developments show that the Sunday pivot has not yet become policy. The White House is leaving open the possibility of talks with Democrats while reaffirming enforcement and moving ahead with construction. Continuity will depend on whether the administration produces a specific legislative offer.

The fifth story is the market’s rebound ahead of this morning’s inflation report. The S and P 500 jumped 2.3 percent Monday, its best day since April. The Dow rose 2.2 percent, and the Nasdaq gained 2.7 percent. Asian markets followed higher overnight, while oil declined.

The rally recovered much of last week’s technology-led selloff, but the consumer-price report at eight-thirty Eastern can change the tone. Economists expect the twelve-month headline rate to rise from 3.7 percent to about 3.9 percent. A hotter number would strengthen the case for another Federal Reserve increase. A softer number would give markets some room to believe that recent energy pressure is not spreading as quickly through the economy.

That is the national brief. Now to the Debt Desk.

The latest official Treasury close is Monday’s. The 2-year finished at 4.56 percent, the 5-year at 4.67, the 10-year at 4.88 and the 30-year at 5.26. Compared with Friday, the 2-year rose five basis points, the 5-year rose three, the 10-year rose two and the 30-year was unchanged.

The curve is still upward sloping, but Monday’s movement was concentrated at the front. The 5-year is eleven basis points above the 2-year. The 10-year is thirty-two basis points above it, and the 30-year is seventy basis points above it. That front-end rise is the market preparing for inflation risk and a Federal Reserve that has not declared victory.

For property finance, the 5-year remains the practical center of the curve. Many bank, life-company, agency and CMBS loans use five-year structures. At 4.67 percent before adding a credit spread, the base rate alone keeps fixed coupons elevated. The unchanged 30-year says the long end already carries a heavy term premium and did not need to reprice further Monday.

Latest published SOFR is 3.89 percent, effective November sixth. That is down three basis points from the prior reading and eight basis points from November third. A floating-rate loan at SOFR plus 300 basis points begins around 6.89 percent before floors, fees and rate-cap costs. At SOFR plus 400, it begins around 7.89 percent. The decline is welcome, but it does not solve a capital stack built for much cheaper money.

The strongest new lending signal is a market split that became clearer Monday evening. Trepp estimates that office and apartment loans running out of extensions over the next twelve months face a combined refinancing gap of nearly 19 billion dollars. About 16 and a half billion dollars of maturing CMBS office debt is in the pool, and more than one-third would require new equity under a 7 percent refinancing assumption.

The apartment wall is larger. Roughly 160 billion dollars of apartment loans mature over the next year, and about 43 percent cannot refinance at today’s rates without additional cash. Trepp estimates a 17 billion dollar gap before accounting for bank extensions. Because banks hold about 84 billion dollars of the apartment maturities and historically extend about half, the bank-related shortfall could narrow to roughly 5 to 11 billion dollars.

At the top of the market, however, lenders are competing intensely. Trepp’s survey of mostly life-company lenders shows quoted spreads at record lows. CBRE says fixed-rate commercial mortgage spreads averaged 197 basis points over Treasuries in the third quarter, twenty-three basis points tighter than a year earlier.

That is the paradox. Spreads are tightening for stabilized assets with durable cash flow, while total coupons remain high because Treasury yields are elevated. A clean loan may receive aggressive bids. A weak office property, a floating-rate apartment loan or an asset that needs every dollar of its old proceeds may struggle to get refinanced at any conventional price.

Banks are part of that competition, especially when the borrower can provide deposits and a broader relationship. Some banks want deposits equal to 10 or 20 percent of the loan amount. That can justify a thinner mortgage spread, but borrowers should treat the deposit requirement as part of the economics. Banks also reported tighter standards across every commercial real estate category in the third quarter.

Life companies are using their long-duration capital to compete for low-leverage, stabilized properties. They can offer fixed-rate certainty and clean execution, but they remain disciplined about proceeds and property quality. Office spreads have not tightened with the rest of the market.

Debt funds and other alternative lenders captured 48 percent of nonagency commercial real estate loans in the third quarter, up from 37 percent a year earlier. Banks’ share fell to 26 percent. Private credit can provide future funding, speed and flexible structure, but there is a constraint behind the growth: many debt funds finance themselves with bank credit lines, and banks have tightened standards for lending to nonbank lenders.

A fresh multifamily execution illustrates where that capital is going. Newmark arranged a 47.6 million dollar refinancing for The Clark, a 170-unit mixed-income property in Brooklyn’s Prospect Lefferts Gardens neighborhood. Benefit Street Partners provided the loan. The building includes market-rate, rent-stabilized and affordable apartments, a long-dated tax abatement and fully leased ground-floor retail.

That is a debt-fund refinance on a completed, diversified apartment asset rather than a rescue loan. The tax benefit, mixed-income profile and occupied retail support the cash flow story. It also shows that private lenders are not limited to high-risk bridge deals; they can compete on stabilized multifamily when the collateral and sponsorship are strong.

CMBS had its largest private-label week since early October. Four deals totaling 4.95 billion dollars priced in the week ended November sixth. The headline was Blackstone’s 3.34 billion dollar financing of an Apartment Income REIT portfolio, the largest private-label CMBS transaction of 2026. The collateral includes 29 apartment properties and 9,389 units across eight states and Washington, D.C. The portfolio was 94.2 percent occupied in October.

The financing came from a broad bank group led by Goldman Sachs, with Bank of America, Barclays, Citigroup, JPMorgan, RBC and Scotiabank. It demonstrates how balance-sheet banks and securitization work together: banks originate the loan, then the CMBS market distributes the exposure.

The same week included another 549 million dollar floating-rate multifamily single-borrower deal, a 260 million dollar fixed-rate self-storage deal and an 805 million dollar ten-year conduit. Floating-rate single-borrower spreads have averaged SOFR plus 220 basis points this year, fourteen basis points tighter than 2025. Senior bonds can clear efficiently, but riskier conduit bonds are wider. Trepp places the riskiest investment-grade CMBS spread around 540 basis points over Treasuries, up from roughly 480 in early September.

Agency securitization added 3.6 billion dollars for the week, including the first ten-year Freddie Mac K-deal since October fourteenth. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac remain essential for permanent multifamily liquidity, and their securitization machine gives lenders a repeatable way to recycle capital. Borrowers still face the same base-rate problem, so proceeds depend on debt-service coverage, property cash flow and the timing of the Treasury lock.

The agency channel is strongest for stabilized conventional apartments, affordable housing and mission-aligned preservation. For loans that do not yet qualify, the bridge-to-agency strategy still works only if the bridge term, rate cap and extension tests leave enough time to complete the business plan.

HUD and FHA remain the long-duration alternative for construction, substantial rehabilitation and affordable housing. The current program development is still the express lane for qualifying low-income housing tax credit loans under Section 221 d 4. HUD is targeting a 30-day path from application to firm commitment, has removed the 200-unit cap and includes qualifying 4 percent tax-credit projects. There was no newly disclosed commitment Monday, so the next evidence will be an actual closing or firm commitment that proves the timetable.

The concise markets snapshot is this. The official curve closed Monday at 4.56 percent on the 2-year, 4.67 on the 5-year, 4.88 on the 10-year and 5.26 on the 30-year. Latest SOFR is 3.89 percent. The S and P 500 rose 2.3 percent Monday, the Dow gained 2.2 percent and the Nasdaq added 2.7 percent. Oil moved lower as markets responded to the possibility of Iran de-escalation.

One thing to watch is the eight-thirty inflation release. The first move should appear in the 2-year and 5-year, then flow into fixed-rate loan quotes and proceeds. Borrowers with a live closing should know whether the lender spread is locked, whether the Treasury index is locked and what happens if the base rate moves ten or twenty basis points. In this market, a competitive spread does not protect a deal from a volatile index.

That is the Debt Desk for Tuesday. Have a good morning.

item.title: Debt Desk — Debt Desk — November 9, 2026: Washington Pivots as Credit Markets Face the CPI Test
item.description: Trump softens his immigration message after the midterms, diplomats tackle Iran and Ukraine, and markets recover from an AI-led selloff. Debt Desk covers the full Treasury curve, SOFR, fresh private-credit and agency executions, CMBS conditions, Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and HUD.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It is Monday, November ninth.

The national brief begins with President Trump’s first major interview since Republicans lost control of both chambers of Congress. The president said his deportation policy may have been too tough for voters, and he raised the possibility of working with Democrats on an immigration agreement.

That is a notable change in tone, though not yet a change in policy. Trump built much of his political identity around aggressive immigration enforcement. Now he is acknowledging that the approach may have contributed to the midterm result. Any bipartisan deal would still have to bridge large disagreements over border enforcement, legal status and the treatment of people already in the country.

The personnel story from the weekend also changed quickly. Trump said Sunday that he was joking when he announced that he had offered UFC chief Dana White the press secretary job. White is therefore not expected at the White House today for an appointment meeting. The serious transition remains Stephen Miller’s move into the chief of staff role as the administration prepares for a Democratic Congress and a more difficult oversight environment.

The larger message from voters was economic. Inflation is running at 3.7 percent over the past year, and the cost of food, housing, energy and credit remains the central political problem. Democrats won a governing mandate in Congress, but they do not have a simple way to lower prices. Trump retains the veto, and measures that stimulate demand could make inflation harder to contain. The areas with some room for negotiation include permitting, health care costs and selected tariff relief. The next Congress will also have to confront federal funding before the current measure expires on December eleventh.

The second story is the Iran war and the effort to restart diplomacy. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Sunday that the conflict was not necessarily popular, but argued that it was required to prevent a nuclear threat. He also said negotiations are not close to a breakthrough.

President Trump is scheduled to meet Qatar’s prime minister at the White House today. Qatar has presented proposals aimed at narrowing the gap between Washington and Tehran. Iran is seeking an end to the port blockade, sanctions relief, access to frozen assets and compensation for war damage. Trump has said renewed strikes are unlikely if talks show real progress, while also warning that the United States has identified additional targets.

The immediate economic connection is energy. Disruption around the Strait of Hormuz has helped lift fuel costs and feed inflation. That means diplomacy is not only a foreign-policy story. It can affect household budgets, Tuesday’s inflation debate and the path of interest rates.
